disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention that interferes with functioning or development, with relatively fewer or no prominent hyperactive-impulsive symptoms. Individuals often have longstanding difficulties with sustained focus, organization, following through on tasks, and managing details, though these issues may not become clinically significant until environmental demands exceed their compensatory strategies. In adults and older adolescents, the disorder commonly presents as chronic disorganization, mental distractibility, and forgetfulness rather than overt behavioral disruption, and may be misattributed to stress, personality traits, or normal aging. Diagnosis requires symptom onset in childhood, cross-situational impairment, and careful differentiation from cognitive disorders, mood and anxiety disorders, or effects of medical illness and substances.

narrative.stressor: For most of her life, Lissette’s meticulous approach to cooking, gardening, and running church events allowed her to mask long‑standing distractibility and reliance on written lists. About a year and a quarter ago, her husband developed more complex health needs, and she took on coordinating his appointments, medications, and insurance in addition to her usual senior center volunteering. The added caregiving responsibilities, with more phone calls, paperwork, and time‑sensitive details, overwhelmed the informal systems she had relied on for decades, leading to mounting errors in scheduling and missed follow‑through that she initially blamed on "getting old." After a near‑miss where she confused her husband’s medication timing and a friend at church gently pointed out similar patterns in her volunteer work, her primary care physician referred her for a psychiatric evaluation to sort out whether this was early dementia or a longstanding attention problem becoming more visible.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep forgetting everyday things—calls I promised to make, appointments I just wrote down, even simple errands—and it’s starting to cause problems with my husband’s care.”

narrative.stressor: Paul had managed through high school and community college by cramming before exams and leaning on his strong memory for big‑picture concepts, so his tendency to mentally drift or misplace materials never drew formal attention. About 15 months ago, his insurance company shifted to a higher‑volume, metrics‑driven workflow that required sustained concentration on long policy documents and precise, repetitive data handling throughout the day. As the workload increased, he found it harder to keep up with the pace and quality standards he needed for promotion, and his supervisor began documenting errors and incomplete files, threatening his path toward becoming a senior adjuster. After a particularly stressful performance review where he was told his "focus and follow‑through" were holding him back despite obvious effort, a coworker who had been evaluated for ADHD suggested he get assessed, prompting Paul to seek psychiatric care when self‑help strategies and extra hours at his desk didn’t improve his consistency.
narrative.chief_complaint: “When I have to sit and focus on these long claim files, my mind just checks out and I end up putting them off or staring at the screen instead of getting them done.”

narrative.stressor: Deborah built a reputation as the "organized one" at her office by relying on color‑coded calendars, checklists, and staying late when needed, which compensated for how much effort it took her to keep track of details. About a year and three months ago, her company reorganized and she was promoted into a more demanding administrative role while she and her spouse were also adjusting to a recent move and added church and community commitments. The cumulative demands—managing more executives’ schedules, remembering shifting deadlines, and juggling home and volunteer responsibilities—pushed her beyond what her usual systems could handle, leading to noticeable lapses in task tracking that threatened her chances at an eventual Office Manager role and caused friction with colleagues who were surprised by her sudden inconsistency. Feeling alarmed that her identity as the dependable, detail‑oriented assistant was slipping and worried she might lose her promotion if this continued, she sought a psychiatric evaluation after her manager suggested that she "seems scattered" and recommended talking to a professional about stress and possible attention issues.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to keep my work straight anymore—projects, emails, and deadlines keep getting jumbled and I feel like I’ve lost my ability to stay organized.”
